name: GPP Passwords (SYSVOL Credentials) — Attack & Detection
description: Group Policy Preferences stored credentials (cpassword) in SYSVOL XML files, encrypted with a publicly known AES key. Any authenticated domain user can read SYSVOL and decrypt passwords. Patched in 2014 (KB2962486) but legacy deployments still contain credentials. Detection: Event 4663 (file access) on the XML file, then 4624/4625/4768 on subsequent logon attempts.
notes:
=== BACKGROUND ===
  SYSVOL path: \\<DOMAIN>\SYSVOL\<DOMAIN>\Policies\
  GPP XML files: Groups.xml, Services.xml, Scheduledtasks.xml, etc.
  Encrypted field: cpassword (AES-256 with published key)
  Microsoft published the AES key on MSDN — anyone can decrypt
  Patch KB2962486 (2014): prevents NEW credentials from being stored
  BUT: does NOT clear existing stored credentials from before 2014

=== ATTACK ===
# PowerSploit Get-GPPPassword — parses all XMLs in SYSVOL, decrypts cpassword
Import-Module .\Get-GPPPassword.ps1
Get-GPPPassword
  → Output: UserName, Password (cleartext), File path, cpassword (encrypted)

  Example output:
    UserName  : svc-iis
    Password  : abcd@123
    File      : \\EAGLE.LOCAL\SYSVOL\eagle.local\Policies\{GUID}\Machine\Preferences\Groups\Groups.xml

=== DETECTION ===
Event 4663: Object Access — generated when SYSVOL XML file is accessed
  → Enable auditing on the Groups.xml file (Advanced Security Settings → Auditing → Everyone → Read)
  → Any access to the file = 4663 event
  → Most effective if using a DUMMY XML file (no real GPO linked) — any access is suspicious

Event 4624/4625: Successful/Failed logon with the discovered account
  → Service account logins from unexpected machines are suspicious
  → Correlate source IP vs. expected servers for that service account

Event 4768: Kerberos TGT requested with the discovered account
  → Correlate source IP vs. known service locations

Honeypot technique:
  → Leave a fake XML with wrong password in SYSVOL
  → Service account is active with recent (simulated) logins
  → Password last changed BEFORE the file's last-modified date
  → Any login attempt (4625, 4771, 4776) → alert (honeypot triggered)

=== PREVENTION ===
  → Apply KB2962486 (if not already patched)
  → Audit SYSVOL for existing cpassword entries regularly
  → Remove/clean any XML files containing cpassword

Get-WinEvent to monitor 4663 (file access) on DC

references.title: Microsoft - MS14-025: Vulnerability in Group Policy Preferences

recommended.note: Credentials also commonly found in network share scripts and config files.

defense.why_it_works: Group Policy Preferences stored a cpassword in SYSVOL XML files, encrypted with an AES key Microsoft published on MSDN. Any authenticated user can read SYSVOL and decrypt it. The 2014 patch (KB2962486) stops NEW cpassword storage but does not remove pre-existing entries.
defense.prerequisites: Any authenticated domain user (SYSVOL is world-readable) and a legacy GPP XML still containing a cpassword.
defense.impact: The cleartext password of the account in the XML (often a service or local-admin account), immediately usable for authentication.
defense.detection: Event 4663 (object access) on the SYSVOL Groups.xml when file auditing is enabled — most effective on a dummy XML with no linked GPO, where any access is suspicious. Then Event 4624/4625 (logon) and 4768 (TGT) for the discovered account from unexpected machines.
defense.artifacts: 4663 access events on GPP XML files; Get-GPPPassword (PowerSploit) execution; a honeypot XML with a fake password firing 4625/4771/4776 on any login attempt.
defense.prevention: Apply KB2962486 if not already patched; audit SYSVOL for existing cpassword entries and remove/clean any XML containing them.
defense.misconfiguration: Group Policy Preferences (GPP) allowed administrators to push local administrator credentials to machines via XML files stored in SYSVOL (\\domain\SYSVOL\...). These files were encrypted with AES-256, but Microsoft published the static key in MSDN documentation. Any authenticated domain user can read SYSVOL, so any account configured this way has its password exposed to every domain user. MS14-025 (KB2962486, May 2014) removed the GUI option but left existing files in place.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# SYSVOL Group Policy file containing encrypted password:
# Path: \\corp.local\SYSVOL\corp.local\Policies\{GUID}\Machine\Preferences\Groups\Groups.xml
# Content:
# <Properties action='U' userName='Administrator' cpassword='edBSHOwhZLTjt...' />
# The cpassword value is AES-256 encrypted with the static key Microsoft published:
# Key: 4e 99 06 e8 fc b6 6c c9 fa f4 93 10 62 0f fe e8 f4 96 e8 06 cc 05 79 90 20 9b 09 a4 33 b6 6c 1b
# gpp-decrypt or Get-GPPPassword decrypts it instantly
defense.secure_config:
# 1. Apply MS14-025 (KB2962486) — blocks new GPP passwords from being created
#    (already applied if any patch from 2014+ is installed)

# 2. Find and delete all existing cpassword entries in SYSVOL:
# PowerShell — find all GPP files with cpassword:
Get-ChildItem -Path '\\corp.local\SYSVOL' -Recurse -Include '*.xml' |
    Select-String -Pattern 'cpassword' | Select-Object Path
# Then delete or edit those files to remove the cpassword attribute

# 3. Rotate any passwords that were stored in GPP immediately
# (assume all were read by every domain user since GPP file creation)

# 4. Use LAPS instead of GPP for local admin passwords:
# LAPS stores unique per-machine passwords in a protected AD attribute
# Only members of a specific group can read the LAPS attribute
